overview: A’uwẽ, often called Xavante, are a Jê-speaking people with communities in Mato Grosso, Brazil. Their communities share language, ceremonial life and forms of social organisation while retaining political autonomy. Histories of migration, outside contact and land loss differ between communities; they are not a single kingdom with one founding or fall date.

periods.title: Different encounters with a moving frontier
periods.summary: One local Xavante group established sustained relations with Brazil’s Indigenous Protection Service in 1946. Other groups followed different paths through the next two decades, amid disease, settlement and missionary activity.

periods.title: Displacement at Marãiwatsédé
periods.summary: The Marãiwatsédé community was removed to São Marcos in 1966 after ranching encroached on its land. Displacement separated families from their territory and was accompanied by devastating disease.

periods.title: Recognition without full return
periods.summary: Marãiwatsédé territory was formally recognised in 1998, but occupation and legal challenges continued to prevent the community’s full return.

periods.title: A partial return
periods.summary: Some Marãiwatsédé families returned in August 2004, but regained access to only part of their territory. Occupation and legal disputes continued.

periods.title: Rebuilding at Marãiwatsédé
periods.summary: Removal of non-Indigenous occupants was completed in January 2013. The community celebrated the recovery while demanding support for food production, health, education and protection of the land.

items.text: In Sereburã’s recollections of childhood, families travelled through the landscape to hunt and gather. Young people learned by watching adults. Scouts also brought fresh maize from village gardens to people on trek, connecting cultivation with mobile food gathering.

At Pimentel Barbosa and Etênhiritipá, Welch describes maize loaves, wild roots, macaúba and game as important ceremonial gifts. Producing and sharing food helped sustain obligations between people, even as purchased foods became more common in daily meals.

Welch records growers experimenting with soils and fallow periods after larger gardens became necessary. Some women recalled selecting and exchanging maize kernels by colour to maintain preferred varieties. Their explanations of declining maize vigour were hypotheses rooted in observation, not a single experimentally established cause.

Xavante bag baskets in the Museu Índia Vanuíre are woven from buriti palm fibre, with lids and carrying straps. The catalogue records vertical twisted weaving and different sizes made for personal use and sale. Construction joins plant knowledge with the needs of carrying and storing.

The same museum’s Xavante sieve has an open woven surface reinforced by wooden rods and cotton bindings. Its catalogue identifies use in sifting maize, bean and sweet-manioc flour. The spacing of the weave makes a working surface for preparing food.

A wooden mortar catalogued as made in 1988 survives in the Museu Nacional dos Povos Indígenas. It is hollowed from a wooden cylinder, with a shaped base. This particular utensil preserves evidence of woodworking for household processing.

A 2021 gathering of Xavante women included collecting buriti leaves and making baquité baskets used in daily tasks and for carrying children. Making objects together provided a practical setting for transmitting skills across generations.

At the 2017 Ripá seed fair, families exchanged maize, bean, gourd, cotton and tree seeds. They discussed the loss of locally maintained varieties when seed saving gave way to annual purchases. The fair connected cultivation with retaining control over planting material.

Women collectors from Ripá prepared native Cerrado seeds for sale to restoration projects. Hunters shared information about where trees were fruiting, helping collectors plan their work. Different forms of landscape knowledge contributed to both income and restoration.

Chief Carolina Rewaptu described family plots producing maize, rice, beans and squash. Participants linked food production with the space needed for hunting, gathering, fishing and cultivation. Seed exchange addressed a wider problem of restricted access to territory.

Mário Juruna became Brazil’s first Indigenous federal deputy. The Chamber of Deputies preserves his April 19, 1983 speech. This record places a Xavante leader’s own public voice within the national parliamentary archive.

ending.text: A’uwẽ communities continue to transmit language, organise ceremonies and defend their territories. Colonial expansion and state policies transformed their autonomy and livelihoods. Marãiwatsédé’s recovery in 2013 was one major community achievement, followed by the work of rebuilding life on damaged land; it was not the end of Xavante history.
